texts.preamble: Mayank Jain vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 9 December, 2015 1 W.P. No.8135/2015 9.12.2015 Shri M.A. Mansoori, learned counsel for the petitioner. This writ petition has been filed by the petitioner challenging the tender conditions and seeking a direction to the respondents to decide the petitioner's representation in this regard. The brief facts are that the respondent No.2 has issued the tender (Annexure P/1) for the supply of items, such as Tent, Food, Light, Sound, equipments for use in various programs/camps and Government functions in the Dhar District for the financial year 2015-16. The petitioner has the grievance in respect of certain conditions of the said tender. Hence this writ petition has been filed by the petitioner challenging the tender conditions. Learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that the tender conditions No.A-5 & A-6 have been incorporated to exclude the petitioner from the competition and to favour certain persons, therefore, they are required to be deleted. He has further submitted that the petitioner's representation in this regard has not been decided till now. Having heard the learned counsel for the petitioner and on the perusal of the record, it is noticed that the petitioner is challenging the following two tender conditions :- "fufonk izLrqrdrkZ QeZ dks foxr 3 o"kksZa He has also failed to point out if the public interest is adversely effected Mayank Jain vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 9 December, 2015 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106057766/ 1 The Supreme Court in the matter of Michigan Rubber (India) Limited Vs. State of Karnataka and others, reported in (2012) 8 Scc 216 while considering the limited scope of interfering in the tender conditions, has held as under :- "23. From the above decisions, the following principles emerge: ( a ) the basic requirement of Article 14 is fairness in action by the State, and non- arbitrariness in essence and substance is the heartbeat of fair play. These actions are amenable to the judicial review only to the extent that the State must act validly for a discernible reason and not whimsically for any ulterior purpose. If the State acts within the bounds of reasonableness, it would be legitimate to take into consideration the national priorities; (b) fixation of a value of the tender is entirely within the purview of the executive and courts hardly have any role to play in this process except for striking down such action of the executive as is proved to be arbitrary or unreasonable . If the Government acts in conformity with certain healthy standards and norms such as awarding of contracts by inviting tenders, in those circumstances, the interference by Courts is very limited; (c) In the matter of formulating conditions of a tender document and awarding a contract, greater latitude is required to be conceded to the State authorities unless the action of tendering authority is found to be malicious and a misuse of its statutory powers, interference by Courts is not warranted; (d) Certain preconditions or qualifications for tenders have to be laid down to ensure that the contractor has the capacity and the resources to successfully execute the work; and (e) If the State or its instrumentalities act reasonably, fairly and in public interest in awarding contract, here again, interference by Court is very restrictive since no person can claim fundamental right to carry on business with the Government.
